---
title: "Methodology"
---

How every number on this site is made, in enough detail to reproduce one. The code is in the
[repository](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence); each step below names
the file that does it.

## The pipeline

Every scheduled run goes through the same six steps.

1. **Collect.** One small script per source fetches the latest file or API response and
   saves it untouched, with the retrieval time, the URL and a checksum.
2. **Validate.** A schema check confirms the columns, types and value ranges look right. If
   they do not, the run stops and opens a GitHub Issue, and the site keeps showing the last
   good data.
3. **Transform.** Raw files become tidy tables: one row per entity per date, standard units,
   standard names.
4. **Model.** Baselines, regressions and residuals are computed from the tidy tables.
5. **Export.** Each page gets a small JSON file under `data/v1/` holding only what it shows,
   with its own label: source, retrieval date, frequency, typical lag and known limitations.
6. **Build and deploy.** Quarto renders the pages from those files and the workflow
   publishes them.

Raw responses are never edited and never published. Fixes happen in transform code, so any
number can be rebuilt from its source. The files under
[`data/v1/`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/tree/main/site/data/v1)
are a contract: pages read only from them, by fixed paths and fixed column names.

## Rules the pipeline enforces

1. **Baseline before model.** Every model page shows a naive comparison. A model that does
   not beat it is published as "no signal found", which is a result.
2. **Split by time, never at random.** Train on the past, test on what came after.
3. **Write the test before looking at outcomes.** Split dates and thresholds are committed in
   code before the first result is seen.
4. **Count the attempts.** Everything tried is listed in the [failures log](failures.qmd).
5. **Respect small samples.** Prefer the simpler model when the gap is within noise.
6. **Never mix incomparable measurements.** Different benchmark versions, listing and
   transaction prices, base and peak scores: separate columns, never averaged together.
7. **Label every number.** The label comes from the metadata file, so it cannot be forgotten.
8. **Say what kind of finding it is.** Every finding carries one of the three labels below.

## Finding labels

Each finding on this site is tagged with what kind of claim it is. The tag is set in code from
the test result, never typed by hand on a page
([`pdi/common/findings.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/pdi/common/findings.py)).

| Label | What it means | What it does not mean |
|---|---|---|
| [Observation]{.finding .finding-observation} | A measured value, or simple arithmetic on measured values, such as score divided by price. No model is involved. | It says nothing about why, or about what comes next. |
| [Explanation]{.finding .finding-explanation} | A fitted model describes a relationship, such as how score rises with core count, or what is left over after it. | The model has not shown it predicts data it never saw better than the naive baseline, so it is a description, not a forecast. |
| [Prediction]{.finding .finding-prediction} | A model's output, published only because that model beat the naive baseline on data it never saw, by more than the noise level fixed before the test. | It is not certain. The page shows the size of its typical error. |

A finding moves up to **prediction** only by passing its module's out-of-sample test. If a
later run fails the test, the label drops back on that run, automatically.

## Tech Value

### Benchmarks

Two open benchmark sources are used for two different jobs, and their scores are never
combined.

- **SPEC CPU 2017** results are submitted by hardware vendors under a published run rule, and
  each one discloses the full tested configuration. That makes them the ground truth for the
  specification model. They are dominated by servers. One suite and one metric are used:
  **SPECrate 2017 Integer, base**.
- **Blender Open Data** is crowd-submitted and covers consumer CPUs and graphics cards. It is
  used for the value ranking. A launch counts only if it used a single device and finished all
  three standard scenes; its score is the sum of samples per minute over those scenes. Scores
  are grouped by device, compute backend and Blender version, a group needs at least five
  runs, and the ranking uses a single Blender version.

### Prices

Prices are collected once a day by a crawler that searches each retailer for each benchmarked
model. A retailer is used only if its robots.txt allows the page and it answers a client that
says what it is; the crawler waits between requests and does nothing to get past a bot wall.
Most large US retailers block automated clients, so coverage is a small part of the market
and is listed on the [sources page](sources.qmd). The price of a model is its cheapest new
listing that is in stock on the collection date. Refurbished and open-box listings and
accessories are left out. These are listing prices, not what anyone paid. Daily prices cannot be
backfilled, so the history starts on the day the collector was switched on.

Once a week, Amazon US and Best Buy listings are added from a data provider, Bright Data.
Amazon's conditions of use exclude collecting and reusing its prices, and Best Buy's rows are
treated the same way, so the raw rows from both are kept out of the public repository. Only the lowest price per model, its history and the fair price
built from it are published.

Amazon's data has no field for a listing's condition, so only new stock that can be vouched
for is counted: a listing must be sold by Amazon.com itself or by the part's own brand. Every
marketplace seller is left out, because a used part offered under a new-looking listing cannot
be told apart from a new one. Listings filed under "Amazon Renewed" or sold by Amazon Resale
are dropped as well. The cost is coverage: older parts that Amazon no longer stocks have no
Amazon price.

Best Buy's search is loose and returns other models and whole PCs beside the part asked for.
A Best Buy listing counts only if Best Buy files it as a bare processor or graphics card,
Best Buy is the seller, the title does not mark it refurbished, open-box or pre-owned, and
its name parses to exactly the model searched for.

Retail listings and benchmark devices are matched by a model key parsed from their names
(`pdi/tech_value/names.py`). A name that is not recognised is left unmatched and counted on the
coverage table. Nothing is matched by guesswork.

### The model

The target is the log of the SPEC score of one published result.

- **Naive baseline:** score is proportional to cores times clock speed. One constant is fitted.
- **Plain regression:** ordinary least squares on log cores, log clock speed, log chips,
  multithreading, log cache per core (L2 and L3), vendor, and years since 2017 at first
  availability.
- **AutoGluon Tabular:** trains boosted trees, random forests and ensembles of them on the same
  information, on a weekly schedule with a fixed time limit on CPU.

Processors are assigned to a period by the first hardware-availability date they appear with,
so one processor is never on both sides of a split. Models are fitted on the training period.
The validation period ranks them and makes the pick. The holdout, which is the newest
generation, is scored once for the pick and for the two reference models.

The pick has to beat the baseline on the holdout by more than the fold-to-fold spread: the
standard deviation, across expanding time-ordered folds, of the baseline error minus the plain
model error. Otherwise the baseline is published. The current result, the leaderboard and the
split dates are on the [model page](tech-value/model.qmd).

### Residuals

The ranking of over- and under-performers uses out-of-fold predictions from the plain
regression: each processor is predicted by a model fitted without any of its results. A
processor's residual is the median over its results, and it needs at least three.

A residual is not a quality score. SPEC results for the same processor differ with memory,
compiler and operating system, and vendors choose which configurations to submit. The tested
configuration is shown beside each residual so that it can be checked first.

### Reproducing a number

```bash
uv sync --extra site
uv run python -m pdi.tech_value.spec      # collect and tidy SPEC results
uv run python -m pdi.tech_value.export    # fit the plain model and write data/v1/
```

The holdout error of the plain regression in `site/data/v1/tech-value/holdout.json` should
match the model page for the same retrieval date.

## Macro Monitor

### Series

About 25 monthly US series come from FRED, and only those first published by a US federal
agency. The six Southeast Asian economies are covered by the BIS tables of policy rates,
consumer prices, exchange rates and real effective exchange rates, because the BIS puts each
measure on one definition for every country, which is what makes a comparison between
neighbours fair. Malaysia has five more series from its statistics office. The full list is on
the [series page](macro/series.qmd) and in
[`pdi/macro/config.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/pdi/macro/config.py).

Coverage is uneven and the page says so: Vietnam has only its exchange rate in these tables,
Singapore has no policy rate, and national sources for Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam
and the Philippines are not wired in yet.

### How a flag is made

For every series and month:

1. **Move.** For levels (prices, jobs, output, exchange rates), 100 times the change in the
   log of the value, which is close to the percent change. For rates, the change in the rate.
2. **Usual move.** The median move over the previous ten years. For series that are not
   seasonally adjusted, the median move in the same calendar month over those years.
3. **Surprise.** The move minus the usual move.
4. **Spreads.** The surprise divided by the series' usual spread: 1.4826 times the median
   absolute deviation of its surprises over the same ten years, a measure that large past
   shocks do not inflate. For series that rarely move at all, such as policy rates, the
   standard deviation is used.

A reading is flagged at 2.5 spreads or more. Only data before the month being scored is used,
so a flag in the backtest is the flag the rule would have raised at the time, with one
caveat: the values are today's revised figures, not the ones first published.

**Against neighbours.** For each BIS measure, a country's spreads minus the median spreads of
the other Southeast Asian economies in the same month, scored the same way against that gap's
own ten years. It needs at least three other countries reporting that month.

The thresholds, the ten-year window and the rule for whether a flag held were written in the
config file on 15 November 2026, before any flag was computed. Every flag is an observation:
it is arithmetic on published values with no fitted model.

### Forecast test

A flag says a move was large. Whether next month's move can be forecast is a separate
question, tested on the [forecast page](macro/model.qmd) with AutoGluon TimeSeries against
four rules of thumb. Forecasts appear on the site, labelled as predictions, only on runs
where the picked model beat the best rule of thumb on months it never saw.

### Revisions

Macro figures are revised. From its first run the pipeline keeps every value as it was first
seen, with the date, in `data/store/macro/vintages.parquet`, and only ever appends to it.
Once that has a year of history the backtest can be rerun on what was known at the time.

### Reproducing a number

```bash
uv sync --extra site
uv run python -m pdi.macro.collect     # needs no key; FRED_API_KEY is used when set
uv run python -m pdi.macro.export      # computes flags and writes data/v1/macro/
```
